cases.case_name: Becker v. Mayo Foundation
cases.holding: The court held that Minnesota's child-abuse reporting act creates no private civil cause of action against a mandatory reporter who fails to report suspected abuse, because the legislature chose to impose only criminal penalties.
cases.quote: The plain language of the statute indicates that the legislature chose to impose criminal, but not civil, penalties on mandatory reporters who fail to report.

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling Minnesota Supreme Court statement of what a mandatory reporter owes and what happens when the duty is breached — criminal exposure, not civil liability.
relevance.INP-02: It confirms that the reporting statute's enforcement scheme is criminal, so a non-mandated third party who does not report faces no civil consequence either.
relevance.INP-06: A hotline report's legal consequences for the reporter are fixed by statute, which supplies criminal but not civil sanctions for failure to report.
relevance.INP-07: The case arose from a hospital's failure to report suspected abuse of an infant, making it the leading Minnesota authority on medical-encounter reporting duties.
relevance.INP-08: The same statutory analysis governs teachers and school staff, who are mandatory reporters under the identical provision construed here.
relevance.DEC-01: Because failure to report carries no civil remedy, a family harmed by a screen-out cannot sue the reporter, which channels accountability into the agency's own process.
relevance.ACT-06: The case arose from the medical treatment of an injured infant and defines the hospital's reporting obligation when emergency care reveals suspected abuse.

cases.case_name: Kuelbs v. Williams
cases.holding: The court held that Minnesota's Reporting of Maltreatment of Minors Act creates no express or implied civil cause of action for bad-faith reporting or investigation, and that the county defendants' statements were protected by a qualified privilege.
cases.quote: We conclude that there is no express or implied civil cause of action under RMMA for bad faith reporting or investigating child maltreatment.

relevance.INP-01: It forecloses a civil suit against a mandated reporter even on an allegation that the report was made in bad faith.
relevance.INP-02: A voluntary reporter likewise cannot be sued civilly under the reporting act, which the court read as an immunity provision rather than a liability-creating one.
relevance.INP-06: Anonymous and hotline reporters are covered by the same immunity provision, which the court held limits liability rather than creating a cause of action.
relevance.INP-10: The holding extends to the investigating agency, so escalation from screening to investigation is not itself actionable in tort under the reporting act.
relevance.DEC-01: A screened-out or mishandled report gives the subject no damages claim under the reporting statute.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision to accept and pursue an investigation is not civilly actionable under the reporting act even if alleged to be in bad faith.

cases.case_name: Guetter v. Brown County Family Services
cases.holding: The court affirmed an order disclosing the reporter's identity to the subject of a child-abuse report, holding the statute permits disclosure by court order once the assessment is complete and does not require the subject first to prove the report was false and made in bad faith.
cases.quote: Guetter is thus entitled to disclosure of the identity of the reporter upon court order, but the statute is silent as to when such an order should be granted.

relevance.INP-02: It sets the limit of a voluntary reporter's anonymity: confidentiality yields to a court order once the assessment is over.
relevance.INP-06: This is the leading Minnesota authority on when a hotline or anonymous reporter's identity may be unmasked to the person reported.
relevance.FAIL-06: It establishes that reporter-identity data is not absolutely shielded and that a court may compel the agency to disclose it.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the Minnesota rule governing access by a data subject to otherwise-confidential child-protection reporter information.

cases.case_name: S.L.D. v. Kranz
cases.holding: The court held that official and vicarious official immunity protect county child-protection employees only for duties requiring judgment or discretion and not for ministerial tasks, affirming as modified with partial summary judgment for the county.
cases.quote: Official immunity only shields government officials from liability stemming from the performance of duties that require the exercise of judgment or discretion

relevance.INP-10: It draws the line between discretionary screening and investigative judgment, which is immune, and ministerial handling of information, which is not.
relevance.DEC-02: The decision to investigate and how to handle the resulting information is measured against the discretionary/ministerial divide set out here.
relevance.PMC-02: It supplies the Minnesota framework for holding a county financially answerable for negligent handling of child-protection information.

cases.case_name: Fosselman v. Commissioner of Human Services
cases.holding: The court held that maltreatment-based disqualification proceedings against mandated reporters are subject to procedural due process and that making the commissioner's reconsideration the final agency action, with no evidentiary hearing, denied relators due process.
cases.quote: We conclude that disqualification proceedings are subject to the requirements of procedural due process.

relevance.INP-01: Mandated reporters who are found to have failed to report face disqualification, and this case establishes that they are constitutionally entitled to process before that finding sticks.
relevance.INP-07: The relators were health-care facility staff disqualified for not reporting maltreatment observed in a care setting.
relevance.INP-08: The same disqualification machinery reaches school and child-care staff who are mandated reporters.
relevance.INP-09: It is the Minnesota decision holding that a licensing/oversight disqualification apparatus must itself satisfy due process.
relevance.DEC-03: A substantiated maltreatment or disqualification determination cannot be made final on paper review alone.
relevance.PMC-02: It constrains how administrative licensing and audit determinations against individuals may be made final.
relevance.PMC-03: It supplies the due-process baseline any Minnesota review body must meet when it makes adverse maltreatment findings about individuals.
relevance.PMC-06: Any automated or paper-record flagging of individuals for maltreatment must still be followed by a constitutionally adequate hearing.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of Child of M.K.
cases.holding: The court held that parents were entitled to withdraw CHIPS admissions that the county obtained by threatening to withhold needed services, because accepting admissions extracted that way was a manifest injustice.
cases.quote: we conclude that a threat to act in a manner that is not in a child's best interests constitutes a manifest injustice

relevance.INP-04: It describes the juvenile court's role when a county routes a family into a CHIPS proceeding to obtain services, and the limits on what the court may accept.
relevance.INP-05: Parents who approached the county seeking help for their child were pressed into admitting statutory grounds; the court held that coercion unenforceable.
relevance.INP-10: It shows what a Minnesota appellate court will do when escalation from service request to formal CHIPS petition is driven by leverage rather than evidence.
relevance.INP-12: The case turns on what the county may demand of parents as the price of protective intervention for a child in crisis.
relevance.DEC-02: It cabins a county's power to convert a family's service request into an accepted maltreatment case.
relevance.DEC-05: It addresses directly the decision to file a CHIPS petition and take admissions on it.
relevance.DEC-06: It is the Minnesota authority on what happens when the voluntary-services path is foreclosed and families are pushed into court to get help.
relevance.ACT-01: The county conditioned voluntary services on a court admission, which the court held was a manifest injustice.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a published Minnesota reversal of an agency-driven CHIPS adjudication on grounds of coerced admissions.
relevance.OUT-05: It sets out the manifest-injustice basis on which a CHIPS adjudication may be undone and the admissions withdrawn.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of Child of T.L.M.
cases.holding: The court dismissed the appeal as untimely, holding an appeal from a final juvenile-protection order must be served and filed within 20 days of service of notice of filing.
cases.quote: We conclude that the appeal is untimely because it was not perfected within 20 days of the notice.

relevance.FAIL-01: It states the 20-day deadline that governs whether a parent can obtain appellate review of an adverse juvenile-protection order at all.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of J.R.
cases.holding: The court held that the service requirement of Rule 82.02 of the Rules of Juvenile Procedure is jurisdictional and dismissed the appeal because the guardian ad litem was not timely served.
cases.quote: we hold that Rule 82.02 of the Rules of Juvenile Procedure is jurisdictional, and because the appeal was not timely served on the guardian ad litem, dismissal is required

relevance.FAIL-01: This is the Minnesota Supreme Court's holding that defective or late service on the guardian ad litem destroys appellate jurisdiction over a juvenile-protection appeal.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of S.E.P.
cases.holding: Reinstating the termination, the court held that appellate courts closely examine the record to confirm the evidence was clear and convincing, and that the findings on statutory grounds, reasonable efforts and best interests were not clearly erroneous.
cases.quote: But we closely inquire into the sufficiency of the evidence to determine whether it was clear and convincing.

relevance.ACT-02: It applies the clear-and-convincing standard to a court-ordered case plan and the parent's compliance with it.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's statement of the appellate standard applied to a termination of parental rights.
relevance.PMC-01: Its close review of whether case-plan services were actually delivered is the judicial counterpart to federal safety and permanency performance review.

cases.case_name: In re Children of T.A.A.
cases.holding: The court reversed the court of appeals and held that the county's reasonable efforts to reunite were supported by clear and convincing evidence, explaining that reasonable efforts are assessed after statutory grounds and best interests are established.
cases.quote: the appellate court then determines whether there is clear and convincing evidence that the county made reasonable efforts to reunite the family

relevance.DEC-05: It shows that a county must be able to prove its reunification efforts by clear and convincing evidence once it moves a case toward permanency.
relevance.ACT-01: It measures voluntary and offered services against the statutory reasonable-efforts criteria of relevance, adequacy, cultural appropriateness, availability, timeliness and realism.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the leading Minnesota authority on whether a court-ordered service plan satisfies the reasonable-efforts requirement.
relevance.OUT-01: It defines what the county must show about its reunification efforts before permanency can be changed away from reunification.
relevance.FAIL-03: Reasonable efforts is the Title IV-E condition on federal reimbursement, and this case sets Minnesota's judicial test for it.
relevance.PMC-01: The reasonable-efforts findings reviewed here are the same judicial determinations the federal CFSR and IV-E reviews audit.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of R.W.
cases.holding: The court held that parental rights may not be terminated on best interests alone without at least one statutory ground, but affirmed the termination because statutory grounds were established by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: the court of appeals ignored the clear statutory directive that parental rights cannot be terminated in the absence of at least one statutory ground for termination

relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling Minnesota rule that a statutory ground proven by clear and convincing evidence is a precondition to termination, best interests alone never sufficing.
relevance.OUT-05: Where no statutory ground is proven, the petition fails regardless of the court's view of the children's interests.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a Minnesota Supreme Court correction of an appellate court that had upheld a termination on an impermissible basis.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of T.R.
cases.holding: The court held that substance or alcohol use alone does not render a parent palpably unfit and that the county's testing-only response did not amount to reasonable efforts, reversing the termination.
cases.quote: substance or alcohol use alone does not render a parent palpably unfit

relevance.ACT-02: It holds that a case plan consisting largely of drug testing, without services aimed at the underlying problem, is not reasonable efforts.
relevance.ACT-03: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's statement that out-of-home placement premised on substance use alone cannot ripen into termination without more.
relevance.OUT-01: Reasonable efforts toward reunification are always required until the court finds on a prima facie showing that they may cease.
relevance.OUT-05: It is a published reversal where the record did not support the statutory ground alleged.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading recent Minnesota Supreme Court reversal of a county's termination case for failure of reasonable efforts.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of S.Z.
cases.holding: The court held that when parental rights are terminated for palpable unfitness the district court must still determine whether reasonable efforts to rehabilitate and reunify were made, even if the determination is that services would be unrealistic.
cases.quote: provision of reasonable efforts must be evaluated by the court in every case

relevance.INP-05: Even where a family has sought or been offered services informally, the court must independently evaluate whether the agency's efforts were reasonable.
relevance.DEC-06: A county that keeps a family out of court still has its service efforts judicially evaluated if the case later escalates.
relevance.ACT-01: It requires the court, not the agency, to decide whether the services offered were reasonable, which is the check on voluntary case planning.
relevance.ACT-02: This is the foundational Minnesota Supreme Court holding that reasonable-efforts findings are mandatory in every termination case.
relevance.OUT-01: It anchors the reunification obligation: no termination without a judicial evaluation of the agency's rehabilitative efforts.
relevance.FAIL-03: It embeds the federal Title IV-E reasonable-efforts condition into a mandatory Minnesota judicial finding.
relevance.PMC-01: It makes the reasonable-efforts determination a case-by-case judicial record that federal reviewers can audit.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of R.D.L.
cases.holding: The court held that the statutory presumption of palpable unfitness applied to parents whose rights to another child were previously involuntarily terminated is narrowly tailored to a compelling state interest and does not violate equal protection.
cases.quote: We therefore hold that the statute does not violate the equal protection provisions of the United States or Minnesota Constitutions

relevance.OUT-02: It upholds the presumption that drives many Minnesota terminations against parents with a prior involuntary termination.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's equal-protection analysis of a child-protection classification that burdens one group of parents.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of B.J.-M.
cases.holding: Exercising its supervisory power over the Rules of Juvenile Protection Procedure, the court held that a parent's rights cannot be terminated unless the termination petition names that parent as a party to the proceeding.
cases.quote: a parent's parental rights cannot be terminated in the absence of a petition naming the parent as a party to the proceedings

relevance.DEC-05: It fixes the minimum content of the petition that opens a Minnesota juvenile-protection case against a given parent.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of J.M.
cases.holding: The court held that the permanency statute's bar on long-term foster care for children under twelve is unambiguous and does not conflict with the best-interests standard, and that the termination statute requires no finding on a child's adoptability.
cases.quote: we hold that the termination statute does not require assessment of a child's adoptability

relevance.OUT-03: It explains when long-term foster care is and is not an available permanency option under Minnesota's permanency statute.
relevance.OUT-04: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's construction of the statutory limits on keeping a child in long-term foster care rather than moving to permanency.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of R.S.
cases.holding: The court held that neither ICWA nor Minnesota law authorizes transferring pre-adoptive and adoptive placement proceedings for an off-reservation Indian child to tribal court, and reversed the transfer.
cases.quote: with respect to an Indian child not residing or domiciled on the child's tribe's reservation, transfer is limited to foster care placement and termination of parental rights proceedings

relevance.INP-11: This is the Minnesota Supreme Court's controlling statement of how far ICWA's tribal-transfer right reaches for an off-reservation Indian child.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of Children of S.R.K.
cases.holding: The court held that ICWA and MIFPA require qualified expert witness testimony as part of the court's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt determination that continued parental custody is likely to cause serious emotional or physical damage, and affirmed the terminations.
cases.quote: The statute provides that the court's serious-damage determination must be supported by evidence "including testimony of qualified expert witnesses."

relevance.INP-11: It is the controlling Minnesota Supreme Court construction of ICWA and MIFPA's evidentiary requirements once a case is identified as involving an Indian child.
relevance.OUT-02: It sets the heightened beyond-a-reasonable-doubt and qualified-expert-witness requirements that govern termination of parental rights to an Indian child in Minnesota.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of T.T.B.
cases.holding: The court held there was good cause under ICWA to deny transfer to tribal court because the transfer motions were not made promptly after notice and the proceedings had reached an advanced stage.
cases.quote: the district court had good cause to deny the motions to transfer jurisdiction of the case to the tribal court

relevance.INP-11: It supplies Minnesota's good-cause standard for refusing an ICWA transfer, turning on promptness and the stage of the proceedings.
relevance.ACT-04: It governs the timing of tribal intervention when a permanent placement of an Indian child with kin or others is being decided.

cases.case_name: In re Custody of S.E.G.
cases.holding: The court held that good cause to depart from ICWA's placement preferences must rest on one or more of the BIA guideline factors and that a child's need for stability is not equivalent to a need to be adopted, reversing the non-Indian adoptions.
cases.quote: We hold, while good cause may include a child's need for stability, this is not equivalent to a need to be adopted.

relevance.ACT-04: It is the leading Minnesota authority limiting when an agency or court may bypass ICWA's relative and tribal placement preferences.
relevance.OUT-03: It constrains the good-cause showing needed to place an Indian child outside the statutory preference order in a permanency disposition.
relevance.FAIL-05: It corrects a departure from ICWA's placement preferences that would have removed Indian children from Indian placements without adequate justification.

cases.case_name: In re S.G.
cases.holding: The court held that the adoption statute's direction to consider a relative's petition first does not create a substantive preference for relatives over non-relatives in determining best interests, and affirmed the adoption by the foster parents.
cases.quote: the language directing the order of consideration does not require that the district court prefer a relative over a nonrelative in determining the best interests of the child

relevance.ACT-04: It is the controlling Minnesota limit on how far the kinship preference actually goes when a relative and a foster parent both petition.
relevance.OUT-02: It states the standard a Minnesota court applies when choosing between competing adoption petitions after termination.

cases.case_name: In re Petition to Adopt S.T.
cases.holding: The court held that the trial court had jurisdiction over the foster parents' adoption petition even without the Commissioner's consent, rejecting the agency's claim of an absolute veto over placement.
cases.quote: we hold that subdivision 7 grants the trial court jurisdiction over the adoption proceeding absent the Commissioner's consent to an adoption petition

relevance.ACT-04: It confirms judicial power to review an agency's placement choice rather than deferring wholly to the Commissioner's consent.
relevance.OUT-03: It preserves a court's authority to decide permanency for a child in agency custody over the agency's objection.
relevance.FAIL-05: The case arose from a dispute over placement of African-American children and establishes judicial review of the agency's placement preference decisions.

cases.case_name: Rew v. Bergstrom
cases.holding: The court held that granting a 50-year extended order for protection did not violate the respondent's procedural due process rights, but remanded for findings on whether the speech restrictions as to the children were necessary.
cases.quote: we conclude that the district court did not violate Bergstrom's procedural due process rights when it granted the extended OFP to Rew

relevance.ACT-05: This is the Minnesota Supreme Court's leading decision on the due-process and First Amendment limits of a long-term protective order that restricts a parent's contact with his children.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of L.K. and A.S.
cases.holding: The court held that MIFPA's placement preferences favoring Indian persons and tribally approved foster placements do not violate the Equal Protection Clause, and that the district court applied the wrong factors in denying the former foster parents' motion to intervene.
cases.quote: MIFPA's placement preferences, which favor Indian persons and foster placements approved by an Indian tribe, do not violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment

relevance.INP-11: It is the most recent published Minnesota decision upholding the state ICWA analogue against constitutional attack.
relevance.ACT-03: It governs who may be made a party to a Minnesota child-protection case contesting a foster placement decision.
relevance.ACT-04: It upholds the tribal and Indian-family placement preferences that control kinship placement of Indian children in Minnesota.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the controlling Minnesota answer to the claim that Indian-preference placement rules are racial discrimination.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of L.K.
cases.holding: The court held that former foster parents were properly denied permissive intervention and that their third-party custody petition was properly dismissed, so they are not parties to the children's CHIPS case, and it vacated the court of appeals' constitutional ruling.
cases.quote: We hold that the district court did not err in denying appellants' petition for permissive intervention and in dismissing their third-party custody petition.

relevance.DEC-05: It defines who is and is not a party once a CHIPS case is opened, and therefore who may litigate the child's placement.
relevance.ACT-03: It is the controlling Minnesota Supreme Court decision on whether former foster parents can contest a change in a child's foster placement.
relevance.OUT-04: It settles the standing of long-term caregivers to litigate a child's continuing placement and custody through the child-protection case.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of A.I.
cases.holding: The court held that a parent's murder of the children's mother, carrying a prison sentence longer than the children's remaining minority, satisfies the statutory definition of palpable unfitness, and affirmed the termination.
cases.quote: appellant's act of murdering the children's mother, resulting in a prison sentence longer than the children's remaining age of minority, satisfies the statutory definition of palpable unfitness

relevance.OUT-02: It is the Minnesota rule for terminating the rights of an incarcerated parent whose sentence outlasts the children's minority.
relevance.OUT-06: It arises from the death of the children's mother at the parent's hands and defines the consequences for the surviving children's permanency.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of J.K.T.
cases.holding: The court held that a parent's appeal from a termination order remains justiciable after the child's death because collateral consequences attach to the order, and affirmed the termination on the merits.
cases.quote: We conclude that collateral consequences attach to the termination order because it may affect any future termination proceedings against appellant.

relevance.OUT-06: It is the published Minnesota decision addressing what survives when a child in the child-protection system dies during the case.
relevance.FAIL-04: It confirms that a child's death under agency involvement does not extinguish review of the agency's and court's determinations.
relevance.PMC-04: It preserves an appellate record about agency conduct even after a child fatality, which is the raw material for fatality review.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of S.W.
cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of parental rights to Indian children, holding the district court did not err in finding that active and reasonable efforts to reunify had failed and in refusing to invalidate the proceedings for earlier ICWA violations.
cases.quote: We conclude that the district court did not err by finding that active and reasonable efforts failed to reunite the family.

relevance.INP-11: It applies the ICWA and Minnesota Tribal/State Agreement definition of active efforts once a case is identified as involving Indian children.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the published Minnesota application of the heightened active-efforts standard to a court-ordered case plan for an Indian family.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of S.N.R.
cases.holding: The court held that a tribe's determination that a child is a member or eligible for membership conclusively establishes the child's status as an Indian child for purposes of ICWA's adoptive placement preferences, and affirmed summary judgment.
cases.quote: a tribal determination that a child is a member or eligible for membership in that tribe is conclusive evidence that a child is an "Indian child" under section 1915

relevance.INP-11: This is the Minnesota rule for the threshold question that triggers ICWA at all: who decides whether the child is an Indian child.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of E.A.C.
cases.holding: The court held that on a challenge to an ICWA petition for return of custody the agency bears the burden of proving active efforts and the serious-damage finding beyond a reasonable doubt, and remanded for application of that standard.
cases.quote: the burden of proof to determine whether active efforts have been made is beyond a reasonable doubt and rests with the agency responsible for providing the remedial services

relevance.OUT-01: It places the burden on the county to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that active efforts were made before a parent's request to have an Indian child returned may be denied.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the strictest Minnesota statement of the agency's evidentiary burden on the efforts requirement that federal funding is conditioned upon.

cases.case_name: In re Child of A.S.
cases.holding: The court held that a parent may voluntarily transfer permanent legal and physical custody to a relative for good cause, but that on this record the earlier transfer was involuntary and therefore triggered the presumption of palpable unfitness.
cases.quote: because such a transfer of custody is a statutorily approved permanency disposition, we conclude that a parent may voluntarily transfer custody to a relative for good cause

relevance.INP-05: It recognizes the parent-initiated route by which a family can place a child with a relative without a contested adjudication.
relevance.DEC-06: It describes the non-adversarial permanency option available when a family agrees to a relative placement rather than litigating.
relevance.ACT-01: It is the Minnesota authority on voluntary parental action as an alternative to compelled intervention, and on its later consequences.
relevance.ACT-04: It is the leading published Minnesota decision on voluntary transfer of permanent legal and physical custody to a relative.
relevance.OUT-03: It defines the standard and the consequences of kinship permanency by transfer of permanent legal and physical custody.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of J.W.
cases.holding: The court reversed the termination, holding the mother rebutted the statutory presumption of palpable unfitness by introducing evidence that would justify a finding she is not palpably unfit.
cases.quote: We conclude that the district court erred because J.W. rebutted the statutory presumption of palpable unfitness by introducing evidence that would justify a finding that she is not palpably unfit.

relevance.OUT-05: It is the published Minnesota decision explaining how a parent defeats the palpable-unfitness presumption and obtains dismissal of the petition.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a published reversal of a county's termination case where the district court applied the presumption too rigidly.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of T.D.
cases.holding: The court held that the district court properly took judicial notice of, and relied on, a prior involuntary custody-transfer order and that the mother did not introduce sufficient evidence to overcome the resulting presumption of unfitness.
cases.quote: We hold that the district court properly relied on the involuntary-transfer order and that T.D. did not introduce sufficient evidence to overcome the presumption.

relevance.DEC-03: It shows how a prior adverse child-protection determination is carried forward and given presumptive effect in the next case against the same parent.

cases.case_name: Hennepin County Community Services Department v. Hale
cases.holding: The court affirmed the Commissioner of Administration's order requiring the county to correct a social-services report, holding substantial evidence supported the conclusion that the report was inaccurate in finding the abuse allegation substantiated.
cases.quote: there is substantial evidence in the record to support the Commissioner's decision that the contested report was inaccurate in concluding that the report of abuse by Johnston was substantiated

relevance.INP-04: The report at issue was prepared for the district court, and the case governs correction of court-directed social-services data.
relevance.INP-09: It is the Minnesota decision establishing that an independent state administrative body can review and order correction of county child-protection conclusions.
relevance.DEC-01: It shows the remedy when an agency records a substantiated conclusion the record does not support.
relevance.DEC-03: It is the leading Minnesota data-practices route for attacking a substantiated child-abuse conclusion held in county records.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a published reversal of a county's child-protection conclusion through the Data Practices Act rather than juvenile court.
relevance.FAIL-06: It enforces the county's statutory duty to keep data on individuals accurate, complete and current.
relevance.PMC-02: It confirms external administrative authority to audit and correct county child-protection records.
relevance.PMC-03: It illustrates independent review of county child-protection determinations outside the juvenile court system.
relevance.PMC-05: It is the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act framework for a data subject to obtain and correct child-protection records.
relevance.PMC-06: It establishes that recorded agency conclusions are challengeable on the record, which is the legal basis for any external data-driven audit.

cases.case_name: K.D. v. County of Crow Wing
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that emergency removal of a child without a court order is constitutionally permitted when continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child's health or welfare, and affirmed summary judgment for the Minnesota county and officers.
cases.quote: In cases in which continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child's health or welfare, emergency removal of children without a court order is constitutionally permitted.

relevance.INP-03: The case arose from a law-enforcement encounter in Crow Wing County that led to protective custody of a child.
relevance.INP-12: It is the governing Eighth Circuit rule, in a Minnesota case, for when protective custody may be taken without prior judicial authorization.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the controlling constitutional standard for a Minnesota agency's decision to remove before obtaining a court order.
relevance.ACT-05: It defines the imminent-threat showing that justifies protective action short of, or in place of, a court order.
relevance.FAIL-02: It supplies the test by which a Minnesota removal without a court order is judged lawful or unlawful under the Fourth and Fourteenth Amendments.

cases.case_name: Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed injunctive and declaratory relief, holding that the wholesale removal of boarding students on stale ex parte orders or with no order at all, absent exigent circumstances, violated the Fourth Amendment.
cases.quote: Waddle effected the wholesale removal of HCA's boarding students with ex parte orders or no orders at all in the absence of exigent circumstances

relevance.INP-03: It addresses a coordinated law-enforcement and child-welfare sweep and the constitutional limits on such joint action.
relevance.INP-12: It is the Eighth Circuit's leading statement that protective custody without a valid order requires probable cause or exigent circumstances.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the circuit's clearest example of an emergency-removal decision that failed constitutional scrutiny.
relevance.ACT-05: It shows that an ex parte protective order obtained on stale or inaccurate information will not insulate a removal.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling Eighth Circuit precedent defining unlawful removal by a child-welfare investigator.

cases.case_name: Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed dismissal of a Minnesota father's § 1983 claims, holding that a CHIPS petition filed two days after removal followed by a hearing within ten days supplied all the procedural process he was due.
cases.quote: In child removal cases, the meaningful time and manner requirement means that the state must hold a hearing promptly after removal.

relevance.INP-10: It measures the constitutional adequacy of a Minnesota county's investigation and escalation practices against the shocks-the-conscience standard.
relevance.INP-12: It fixes the post-removal hearing timeline that follows an emergency protective custody in Minnesota.
relevance.DEC-02: It holds that conduct during a child-abuse investigation is actionable only if it shocks the conscience, not merely because it was wrong.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the most recent Eighth Circuit decision reviewing a Minnesota county's emergency removal and the process owed afterward.
relevance.ACT-03: It states when a foster placement following removal satisfies due process because a prompt post-deprivation hearing followed.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the leading recent Minnesota-arising § 1983 case on procedural and substantive due process claims for wrongful removal.

cases.case_name: Riehm v. Engelking
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The court held that a Minnesota county social worker's 72-hour protective hold of a student under an ex parte order was objectively reasonable and that the order was not so lacking in probable cause as to make reliance on it unreasonable, granting qualified immunity.
cases.quote: The ex parte order was not so lacking in indicia of probable cause as to render Diercks's reliance on it unreasonable.

relevance.INP-03: The hold followed a coordinated school, police and county response to a student's writings.
relevance.INP-08: The case begins with a school principal's report of a student's threatening essay to county child protection.
relevance.INP-12: It is the Eighth Circuit's application of the protective-custody standard to a Minnesota 72-hour hold under an ex parte order.
relevance.DEC-04: It shows when a caseworker may rely in good faith on an ex parte order to take a child into custody.
relevance.ACT-06: The child was held for emergency psychological evaluation, and the case defines the constitutional limits on that detention.
relevance.FAIL-02: It marks the boundary between a defensible ex parte hold and an unlawful seizure of a child.

cases.case_name: Burton v. Richmond
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of qualified immunity to state caseworkers, holding it was clearly established that children placed in state foster custody have a substantive due process right to protection, medical care and supervision.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we affirm the district court's denial of the Defendants' motion to dismiss based upon qualified immunity.

relevance.ACT-03: It establishes that once the state places a child in foster care it assumes an affirmative constitutional duty of protection and supervision.
relevance.OUT-04: The duty of protection and supervision runs for as long as the state retains custody of the youth.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the Eighth Circuit's authority for liability when a child is seriously harmed in a state-arranged placement.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the controlling circuit precedent for § 1983 liability of caseworkers when a child is harmed while under agency supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: It defines the legal duty whose breach a fatality or serious-injury review is meant to detect.

cases.case_name: James v. Friend
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for child-protection workers after a foster child's death, holding their conduct did not amount to the deliberate indifference required to shock the conscience.
cases.quote: When deliberation is practical, the officials' conduct will not be found to be conscience-shocking unless the officials acted with deliberate indifference.

relevance.ACT-06: It sets the standard for when a failure to obtain or act on medical information about a child in care becomes constitutionally actionable.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the Eighth Circuit's standard for civil liability arising from a child's death while the agency was involved.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines the deliberate-indifference threshold a family must meet to hold caseworkers liable for a child's death under supervision.
relevance.PMC-04: It states the legal standard against which post-fatality reviews of caseworker conduct are ultimately measured.

cases.case_name: Santosky v. Kramer
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before terminating parental rights, and that a fair-preponderance standard is unconstitutional.
cases.quote: Evaluation of the three Eldridge factors compels the conclusion that use of a "fair preponderance of the evidence" standard in such proceedings is inconsistent with due process.

relevance.OUT-02: It is the federal constitutional floor for the burden of proof in every Minnesota termination of parental rights case.

cases.case_name: Radke v. County of Freeborn
cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and reinstating a wrongful-death complaint, the court held that a common-law negligence action may be maintained against a county and its child-protection workers for negligence in the investigation of, and intervention in, reports of suspected child abuse required under the Child Abuse Reporting Act.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we hold that a cause of action can be maintained for negligence in the investigation of child abuse and neglect reports as required under CARA.

relevance.DEC-01: It is the controlling Minnesota authority that closing a report as unfounded is not immune from review: the county here sent the father a letter saying no abuse had occurred, and the child was beaten to death eleven days later.
relevance.DEC-02: Once a county accepts a report and begins an investigation, the manner in which it conducts that investigation is measured against a common-law duty of care owed to the identified child.
relevance.INP-10: It is the leading Minnesota case on what a county owes a child after intake escalates to investigation, arising from four separate reports the county visited and closed without protective action.
relevance.OUT-06: It arises directly from a child fatality during an open county investigation and defines the civil remedy available to the child's next of kin.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's holding that a wrongful-death negligence action lies against a county and its named child-protection workers when a child under active investigation is killed.
relevance.PMC-02: It supplies the Minnesota mechanism by which a county can be held financially answerable for a failed child-protection investigation, independent of any federal audit.

cases.case_name: Valtakis v. Putnam
cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment, the court held that the Child Abuse Reporting Act imposes no duty between a mandated reporter and the abused child that can support a negligence action, so failure to report gives rise to no civil cause of action.
cases.quote: Since CARA created the duty to report, a civil action cannot lie outside the express or clearly implied language of the statute.

relevance.INP-01: This is the original Minnesota holding that a mandated reporter's failure to report supports no private damages action — the first link in the Valtakis / Kuelbs / Becker line that Kuelbs expressly rests on.
relevance.INP-02: Because the duty to report is purely statutory and no common-law duty preceded it, no reporter — mandated or voluntary — is civilly answerable under the reporting act.
relevance.INP-06: It also construes the statute's one-report rule, holding that a probation officer who relayed the information up a chain to police and county social services satisfied the reporting requirement.
relevance.DEC-01: It is the foundation of the no-civil-remedy rule, which Radke later confined to failures to REPORT as distinct from negligence in the county's own investigation.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of G.L.H.
cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals, the court held that a parent's waiver of the statutory right to counsel in a termination trial need not follow the criminal rule's waiver colloquy and may be found voluntary and intelligent from the surrounding circumstances, and that this parent's waiver was valid.
cases.quote: the determination of whether a parent's waiver of counsel in a TPR proceeding is voluntary and intelligent can be based on the surrounding circumstances of the case

relevance.FAIL-01: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's decision on a parent's statutory right to effective assistance of counsel at a termination trial and on the standard an appellate court applies to a claimed invalid waiver, reviewed only for clear error; it corrects this brief's earlier note that no such Minnesota authority was found.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Children of Coats
cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and reinstating the district court's default judgment, the court held that a mother who signed a notice warning that default could be entered, failed to appear at the pretrial hearing, and showed neither a reasonable defense on the merits nor a reasonable excuse was not entitled to Rule 60.02 relief, and that the resulting termination was not void for lack of due process.
cases.quote: Accordingly, we hold that the default judgment is not void for lack of due process.

relevance.ACT-02: The mother's documented non-compliance with a court-ordered case plan across five review hearings — testing, therapy, psychiatric evaluation and an in-home parenting program — was the entire evidentiary basis on which her rights were terminated.
relevance.DEC-05: It fixes what can follow the filing of a petition: a parent served with a notice warning of default who does not personally appear may have the petition granted on the merits at the pretrial hearing, without a trial and after counsel is allowed to withdraw.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of M.D.O.
cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and leaving the trial court's dismissal of the petition in place, the court held the county had not proved palpable unfitness or refusal to comply with parental duties, where it made an admission of culpability the gateway goal of its case plan while itself failing to provide the services and counseling that would have made rehabilitation possible.
cases.quote: The county's expectations seem especially daunting considering the county's admitted failure to provide services, counseling or assistance to aid Ostlund in coming to grips with her conduct.

relevance.ACT-02: It is the foundational Minnesota holding that a case plan whose first and controlling requirement the county never explained, supported with services, or even asked the parent to accept cannot carry a termination.
relevance.OUT-01: A county that has not delivered the services its own plan demands has not done what Minnesota requires before the goal of reunification may be abandoned.
relevance.OUT-05: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's reinstatement of a trial court's dismissal of a termination petition the county failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's foundational correction of an appellate court that ordered termination on a record the trial court had found insufficient, and it is the decision T.R. later builds on.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of the Child of W.L.P.
cases.holding: Affirming both terminations, the court held that a parent's admission to the allegations of an involuntary termination petition does not convert it into a voluntary termination, that a prior involuntary termination therefore triggers the presumption of palpable unfitness, and that in such cases the county is relieved of the obligation to make reasonable efforts to rehabilitate and reunify.
cases.quote: But in cases where the court has previously terminated an individual's parental rights, reasonable efforts for rehabilitation and reunification are not required.

relevance.ACT-01: It marks the statutory exception to voluntary case planning: where a parent's rights to another child were involuntarily terminated, the county need offer no services at all, and the parent must marshal community resources herself to demonstrate fitness.
relevance.OUT-01: It is the express carve-out from Minnesota's otherwise mandatory reunification-efforts requirement and must be read alongside S.Z. and T.R., which state the general rule.
relevance.DEC-03: It holds that an admission to an involuntary petition does not make the resulting termination voluntary, which is what determines whether a prior adverse determination carries the unfitness presumption into the next case.

cases.case_name: In re Welfare of D.L.
cases.holding: Affirming adoption by the child's grandparents over the competing petition of her long-term foster parents, the court declined to reach the equal-protection challenge to the minority-heritage preference statute and held instead that adoptive placement with a relative is presumptively in a child's best interests unless good cause to the contrary or detriment to the child is shown.
cases.quote: adoptive placement with a family member is presumptively in the best interests of a child, absent a showing of good cause to the contrary or detriment to the child

relevance.ACT-04: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's statement of the relative-placement presumption and the necessary counterweight to In re S.G., which narrows the preference at the competing-petition stage; citing S.G. alone gives a practitioner only half the rule.
relevance.OUT-03: It sets the standard when a relative and a non-relative both seek permanency for the same child, and holds that the temporary pain of separating a securely attached child from a good foster home is not good cause to defeat the family preference.
relevance.FAIL-05: The preference at issue applied by its terms only to children of minority racial or ethnic heritage; the court resolved the case on best-interests grounds and expressly declined to decide whether that classification violates equal protection.

cases.case_name: State v. Grover
cases.holding: Reversing the dismissal of the prosecution, the court held that Minnesota's child-abuse reporting statute is neither unconstitutionally vague nor overbroad, and that it reaches a mandated reporter whose failure to report is merely negligent rather than knowing or reckless.
cases.quote: Holding that the statute is not unconstitutionally vague or overbroad, we reverse and remand to the district court for further proceedings.

relevance.INP-01: It is the Minnesota Supreme Court decision sustaining criminal prosecution of a mandated reporter and construing the 'knows or has reason to believe' trigger, and it is the enforcement mechanism Becker later identified as the only one the legislature provided.
relevance.INP-08: The defendant was an elementary-school principal charged with misdemeanors for not reporting parents' complaints that a teacher had pinched, patted and choked their children, making this the leading Minnesota authority on school-based reporting duties.

cases.case_name: Schmidt ex rel. P.M.S. v. Coons
cases.holding: Reversing the court of appeals and vacating the order for protection, the court held that the Domestic Abuse Act authorizes an order for protection only for a victim of domestic abuse, so a father could not obtain one on his son's behalf without a finding that the son was himself a victim.
cases.quote: We hold that an OFP may be granted only to a victim of domestic abuse.

relevance.ACT-05: It is the controlling Minnesota limit on using a protective order to shield a child: absent a finding that the child was himself the victim of domestic abuse, the Domestic Abuse Act supplies no remedy, and the opinion points instead to the juvenile-protection petition under Minn. Stat. §§ 260C.141 and 260C.148.

notes: Method: every case in this brief was retrieved from the CourtListener v4 API on 2026-09-20 (search in courts minn, minnctapp, ca8 and scotus) and its opinion text was downloaded and read. Every quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved majority opinion (whitespace and curly quotes normalized) and is 30 words or fewer. No unpublished or nonprecedential Minnesota decisions were used.

The pre-existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the MN node files are keyword-matched noise with synthetic citations. None were retained. The only overlap with those lists is incidental; each case here was independently searched, retrieved and read.

Statutory recodification warning for INP-01/02/06/07/08 and DEC-01/03: Becker v. Mayo Foundation and Kuelbs v. Williams construe the former Minn. Stat. § 626.556 (the Child Abuse Reporting Act / Reporting of Maltreatment of Minors Act). That chapter was recodified in 2020 as Minn. Stat. ch. 260E. The reporting duty, the good-faith immunity provision and the criminal-only penalty structure carried forward, so the holdings remain good law, but counsel should cite the current ch. 260E provisions alongside them.

Fourth Amendment / emergency removal (INP-12, DEC-04, FAIL-02, ACT-05): no published Minnesota Supreme Court or Court of Appeals opinion was located on warrantless caseworker entry, consent to search in a CPS investigation, or the constitutional standard for seizing a child without a court order. Searches in minn and minnctapp for 'exigent circumstances removal child social worker' and 'search home child protection worker consent warrant' returned nothing on point. Those nodes therefore rest on the Eighth Circuit, which is the controlling federal circuit for Minnesota. K.D. v. County of Crow Wing, Mitchell v. Dakota County Social Services and Riehm v. Engelking all arise from Minnesota counties; Heartland Academy Community Church v. Waddle is a Missouri case but is the circuit's leading statement of the rule and is followed in Riehm.

OUT-04 (Extended Foster Care / Aging Out) is the weakest node in this layer. No published Minnesota appellate decision construing Minn. Stat. § 260C.451 (extended foster care to age 21), the Chafee program, or continued juvenile court jurisdiction past 18 was found; targeted searches for '260C.451', 'extended foster care jurisdiction age 18' and 'foster care benefits eighteen independent living transition youth' returned no on-point published opinions. The node is mapped to the nearest Minnesota authority on the limits of long-term foster care as a permanency option (In re Welfare of J.M.), on standing to litigate a youth's continuing placement (In re Welfare of the Children of L.K. (Minn. 2026)), and to the federal constitutional duty owed to a youth in state custody (Burton v. Richmond). A practitioner should treat the federal statutes (Pub. L. 106-169; Pub. L. 110-351) and § 260C.451 itself as the operative authority here.

FAIL-03 (Federal Compliance Failure) has no Minnesota case law. No published decision was found addressing CFSR penalties, Title IV-E disallowances, or Single Audit Act findings against Minnesota. The node is mapped to the Minnesota reasonable-efforts and ICWA active-efforts cases (T.A.A., S.Z., E.A.C.) because reasonable efforts is the judicial finding on which Title IV-E reimbursement is conditioned; the operative authority is 42 U.S.C. §§ 670-679c and 45 C.F.R. pt. 1355.

The PMC family (PMC-01 through PMC-06) describes federal oversight and Project Milk Carton's own accountability layer, not doctrines Minnesota courts decide. No Minnesota case law exists on CFSR monitoring, CAPTA § 5106a(c) Citizen Review Panels, the Protect Our Kids Act commission, or federal FOIA as applied to state child-welfare data. Those nodes are mapped to the closest real Minnesota authority — the Government Data Practices Act correction and disclosure cases (Hale; Guetter; In re Certain Records of the McLeod County Juvenile Court) and the maltreatment due-process cases (Fosselman; Thompson) — plus the federal fatality-liability standard (Burton; James). PMC-05 is the only PMC node with genuinely on-point Minnesota precedent; the rest should be read as the nearest analogue, with the federal statutes controlling.
Missing children from care: no published Minnesota appellate decision was located on children who run away or go missing from foster placement. That topic is not separately represented in this layer.

Citation-form notes. (1) Cluster 8283781 (911 N.W.2d 821) carries the case_name 'In re' in CourtListener; the case is styled by the reporter as In re Welfare of Children of S.R.K. and O.A.K. and is cited here in that form. (2) Cluster 10809166 (Minn., Mar. 11, 2026) has no reporter citation yet and is cited in slip form with its docket, No. A23-1762; it reviews the published court of appeals decision at 9 N.W.3d 174 (cluster 10707173) and vacated the portion of that decision reaching MIFPA's constitutionality, so the equal-protection holding in In re Welfare of the Children of L.K. and A.S. should be cited with care pending further authority. (3) In re Welfare of the Children of T.R. is dated 2008-07-02 per CourtListener; the opinion was filed May 30, 2008 and modified upon denial of rehearing.

Practice point for DEC-03: Minnesota provides two distinct routes to attack a substantiated maltreatment finding — the administrative reconsideration and contested-case path (Fosselman; Thompson), and correction of inaccurate government data under the Minnesota Government Data Practices Act (Hale). They have different standards and different forums; a family should be advised on both.

Practice point for FAIL-01: Minnesota juvenile-protection appeals are governed by a 20-day deadline that is jurisdictional and that requires service on the guardian ad litem (In re Welfare of J.R.; In re Welfare of Child of T.L.M.). In re Welfare of the Children of N.L. is the exception that restarts the clock when the district court files an amended final order. No published Minnesota decision recognizing an ineffective-assistance-of-counsel claim in a termination proceeding was located in these searches; searches for 'right to counsel ineffective assistance termination parental rights' in minn and minnctapp returned nothing on point.

Missing (for a later pass): Radke v. County of Freeborn, 694 N.W.2d 788 (Minn. 2005) — THE most serious omission. The Minnesota Supreme Court reversed the court of appeals and held that a common-law negligence action CAN be maintained against a county and its child-protection workers for negligent investigation and intervention in reports of suspected abuse under the Child Abuse Reporting Act, in a wrongful-death case brought after a nineteen-month-old was beaten to death during an open county investigation. This is the controlling Minnesota authority for DEC-01, DEC-02, INP-10, FAIL-04 and PMC-02, and it directly contradicts the brief's repeated blanket statements — drawn from Kuelbs (2000) and stretched from Becker — that a screened-out or mishandled report and a bad-faith investigation carry no civil consequence. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 2071545).

Missing (for a later pass): Valtakis v. Putnam, 504 N.W.2d 264 (Minn. Ct. App. 1993) — the original Minnesota holding that the reporting act creates no express or implied civil cause of action. Kuelbs rests on it explicitly ('As stated in Valtakis, we are prohibited from creating causes of action neither expressly nor impliedly recognized by the legislature') and Becker and Radke both engage it. Any INP-01/INP-02/INP-06 or DEC-01 discussion that cites Kuelbs but not Valtakis and Radke is citing the middle of a three-case line. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 2220887).

Missing (for a later pass): In re Welfare of G.L.H., 614 N.W.2d 718 (Minn. 2000) — the Minnesota Supreme Court on a parent's statutory right to counsel at a termination trial and what constitutes a valid waiver of that right. The brief's FAIL-01 practice note states that searches for 'right to counsel ineffective assistance termination parental rights' in minn and minnctapp 'returned nothing on point'; that note is wrong and should be corrected. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 2211527).

Missing (for a later pass): In re Welfare of the Children of Coats, 633 N.W.2d 505 (Minn. 2001) — a leading Minnesota Supreme Court termination decision on statutory grounds (abandonment), reasonable efforts and best interests, decided between S.Z. and T.A.A. and routinely cited alongside R.W. and S.E.P. Its absence from OUT-02 and OUT-05 is conspicuous. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 1985979).

Missing (for a later pass): In re Welfare of M.D.O., 462 N.W.2d 370 (Minn. 1990) — the Minnesota Supreme Court's foundational reasonable-efforts reversal, where the county failed to provide services designed to address the actual barrier to reunification. T.R. relies on it at length, so the brief cites the case that follows M.D.O. without citing M.D.O. It belongs at ACT-02, OUT-01 and FAIL-01. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 2212288).

Missing (for a later pass): In re Welfare of the Child of W.L.P., 678 N.W.2d 703 (Minn. Ct. App. 2004) — the voluntary-versus-involuntary termination and transfer-of-custody 'good cause' decision that In re Child of A.S. is built on and quotes repeatedly, including the rule that an admission to an involuntary petition does not convert it into a voluntary one. Needed at ACT-01, ACT-04, DEC-06 and OUT-03. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 1788439).

Missing (for a later pass): In re Welfare of D.L., 486 N.W.2d 375 (Minn. 1992) — the Minnesota Supreme Court on the statutory relative/kinship placement preference in adoption ('a strong preference for placement with relatives'). It is the necessary counterweight to In re S.G. (2013), which narrows the preference; citing S.G. alone at ACT-04 and OUT-03 tells a practitioner only half the rule. Verified on CourtListener (cluster 2016587).

GAP-CLOSING PASS, 2026-09-20. All seven authorities named by the verifier were located on CourtListener, confirmed Published, and their full opinion text was downloaded and read in this session. None failed verification — there is no authority on the verifier's list that could not be confirmed. Two of the seven were materially mischaracterized in the verifier's description (In re Welfare of the Children of Coats and In re Welfare of the Child of W.L.P.); each is mapped below to the nodes its actual holding supports rather than the nodes the description named. The nine 'Missing (for a later pass)' notes above are retained verbatim as the audit trail, but they are now SUPERSEDED by the entries added in this pass.

Added Radke v. County of Freeborn (694 N.W.2d 788 (Minn. 2005)) for DEC-01, DEC-02, INP-10, OUT-06, FAIL-04 and PMC-02: it is the Minnesota Supreme Court's holding that a common-law negligence action lies against a county and its child-protection workers for a negligent investigation, and it repairs the single most dangerous defect in the prior brief. CORRECTION TO EXISTING ENTRIES: the relevance sentences on Becker (DEC-01: 'a family harmed by a screen-out cannot sue') and Kuelbs (DEC-01: 'a screened-out or mishandled report gives the subject no damages claim'; DEC-02: 'the decision to accept and pursue an investigation is not civilly actionable') are too broad as written. The correct Minnesota rule, after Radke, is two-part: there is NO civil cause of action for failure to REPORT (Valtakis 1993; Kuelbs 2000; Becker 2007), but there IS a common-law negligence action for the county's negligent INVESTIGATION of and intervention in reports it has received (Radke 2005). Radke distinguished Valtakis and Kuelbs on exactly that basis. Counsel and families should read those three entries subject to this note.

Added Valtakis v. Putnam (504 N.W.2d 264 (Minn. Ct. App. 1993)) for INP-01, INP-02, INP-06 and DEC-01: it is the origin of the no-private-right-of-action rule that Kuelbs rests on and that Becker and Radke both engage, so the reporting-liability nodes no longer cite only the middle of the three-case line. It also supplies the statute's one-report rule, which matters to any reporter who passes information to a colleague or supervisor rather than to the agency directly.

Added In re Welfare of G.L.H. (614 N.W.2d 718 (Minn. 2000)) for FAIL-01: it is the Minnesota Supreme Court on a parent's statutory right to effective assistance of counsel in a termination proceeding and on when a waiver of that right is valid. CORRECTION: the FAIL-01 practice-point note above states that searches for 'right to counsel ineffective assistance termination parental rights' in minn and minnctapp 'returned nothing on point.' That statement is wrong and should be disregarded. Note the limit of G.L.H.: the right is statutory, not constitutional, so the criminal waiver colloquy of Minn. R. Crim. P. 5.02 does not apply and the waiver is judged on the totality of surrounding circumstances, reviewed only for clear error.

Added In re Welfare of the Children of Coats (633 N.W.2d 505 (Minn. 2001)) for ACT-02 and DEC-05. IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO THE VERIFIER'S DESCRIPTION: Coats is NOT a decision on abandonment, reasonable efforts and best interests. Having read the opinion, it decides whether a parent who failed to appear at a pretrial hearing may have her rights terminated by default and whether she was entitled to relief under Minn. R. Civ. P. 60.02; the court reversed the court of appeals and reinstated the default judgment over three dissents. It is therefore mapped to DEC-05 (what can follow the filing of a petition) and ACT-02 (case-plan non-compliance as the evidentiary basis), not to OUT-05, where it does not belong. It does bear on OUT-02, but OUT-02 already carries the six-case maximum (Santosky, R.W., S.E.P., R.D.L., A.I., S.R.K.) and no verified entry was removed to make room; a later pass should decide whether A.I. or R.D.L. yields to Coats there. Practice point for families: Coats is the case that shows a parent can lose her children by not appearing at a single pretrial hearing.

Added In re Welfare of M.D.O. (462 N.W.2d 370 (Minn. 1990)) for ACT-02, OUT-01, OUT-05 and FAIL-01: it is Minnesota's foundational reasonable-efforts reversal, in which the county made an admission of culpability the gateway goal of its case plan, never told the incarcerated mother what would satisfy that goal, never contacted her therapy providers, and never asked whether she would comply — and then argued she could not be rehabilitated. T.R. (2008), already in this brief, relies on M.D.O. at length, so the brief previously cited the sequel without the original.

Added In re Welfare of the Child of W.L.P. (678 N.W.2d 703 (Minn. Ct. App. 2004)) for ACT-01, OUT-01 and DEC-03. CORRECTION TO THE VERIFIER'S DESCRIPTION: W.L.P. is not a transfer-of-custody decision. It construes voluntary versus involuntary TERMINATION under Minn. Stat. § 260C.301, subd. 1(a) and 1(b), holding that an admission to an involuntary petition does not convert it into a voluntary one and identifying the two procedures (a new petition citing subd. 1(a), or a formal amendment) by which a parent actually can. In re Child of A.S. (2005) later carried that reasoning across to voluntary transfer of permanent legal and physical custody. For that reason W.L.P. is NOT mapped to ACT-04 or OUT-03. Its most consequential contribution to this brief is the reasonable-efforts exception it states: where a parent's rights to another child were involuntarily terminated, Minnesota law relieves the county of any obligation to develop a case plan or make reasonable efforts — a qualification that must be read against the otherwise categorical statements of S.Z. and T.R. at ACT-01, ACT-02 and OUT-01.

Added In re Welfare of D.L. (486 N.W.2d 375 (Minn. 1992)) for ACT-04, OUT-03 and FAIL-05: it is the Minnesota Supreme Court's relative-placement presumption — adoptive placement with a family member is presumptively in the child's best interests absent good cause or detriment — and is the necessary counterweight to In re S.G. (2013). Two caveats a practitioner must carry: (1) the court expressly held that relatives' adoption petitions are not granted automatically and that the trial court retains broad discretion; and (2) the preference statute construed there, the former Minn. Stat. § 259.28, subd. 2, applied only to children of minority racial or ethnic heritage, and the opinion itself records that 1992 Minn. Laws ch. 557 had just amended it to apply a relative preference regardless of race — so cite the current race-neutral relative-preference provisions, not § 259.28, subd. 2.

Added State v. Grover (437 N.W.2d 60 (Minn. 1989)) for INP-01 and INP-08, to bring INP-08 (Educational Disclosure) to the two-case floor. It is the Minnesota Supreme Court's only decision sustaining a criminal prosecution of a mandated reporter — an elementary-school principal charged with misdemeanors for not reporting parents' complaints about a teacher — and it construes the statute's 'knows or has reason to believe' trigger, holding that merely negligent failure to recognize abuse violates the statute. Grover is the enforcement mechanism Becker later described as the only one the legislature provided, so INP-01 now carries both ends of that proposition.

Added Schmidt ex rel. P.M.S. v. Coons (818 N.W.2d 523 (Minn. 2012)) for ACT-05, to bring the Protective Order node above the floor with a Minnesota Supreme Court authority rather than only federal removal cases. Quoted from the lead opinion by Justice Meyer; Justice Dietzen filed a dissent, which was not used. The practical consequence is significant for families: a parent cannot use an order for protection to keep a child away from an abuser of someone else in the household unless the child himself was a victim, and the opinion directs such families to the juvenile-protection petition route under Minn. Stat. §§ 260C.007, subd. 6, 260C.141 and 260C.148 instead.

Node-map reconciliation, 2026-09-20. In the prior brief several case entries declared relevance for nodes the node_map did not list. Two of those omissions left nodes below the two-case floor and have been repaired: OUT-04 was empty although In re Welfare of J.M., In re Welfare of the Children of L.K. (Minn. 2026) and Burton v. Richmond each already declared OUT-04 relevance, and it now lists those three; INP-04 carried only Hale although In re Welfare of Child of M.K. already declared INP-04 relevance, and M.K. was added. No node was backfilled beyond what was needed to reach the floor, no verified entry was removed, and after this pass every one of the 42 nodes carries between two and six cases. Nodes already at the six-case maximum (INP-11, ACT-02, ACT-04, OUT-01, OUT-02) could not absorb further additions; the affected candidates are named in the notes above.

OUT-04 re-searched on 2026-09-20 and still has no Minnesota authority. A CourtListener search of minn and minnctapp for '260C.451' OR 'foster care until age 21' OR 'extended foster care' returned exactly two published hits, neither on point: In re Welfare of Children of D.M.T.-R., 802 N.W.2d 759 (Minn. Ct. App. 2011), is a UCCJEA jurisdiction case that merely cites the chapter range §§ 260C.001-260C.451, and Wenndt v. Wenndt, 398 N.W.2d 7 (Minn. Ct. App. 1986), is a dissolution case. There is also no United States Supreme Court decision on extended foster care or aging out, so no federal standard could be substituted under the instruction to map the applicable SCOTUS case. OUT-04 therefore rests on the nearest Minnesota analogues (J.M. on the limits of long-term foster care; L.K. (Minn. 2026) on who may litigate a youth's continuing placement) plus Burton v. Richmond for the constitutional duty owed while the state retains custody, with Minn. Stat. § 260C.451 and the federal Chafee provisions (Pub. L. 106-169; Pub. L. 110-351) as the operative authority.

INP-04 (Court-Ordered Referral) has no published Minnesota decision squarely holding that a judge may direct CPS to investigate. Searches on 2026-09-20 in minn and minnctapp for court-ordered county child-protection investigations arising in dissolution, custody and criminal proceedings returned nothing on point. The node rests on Hale (correction of a social-services report prepared for the district court) and M.K. (the juvenile court's role, and its limits, when a county routes a family into CHIPS); Schmidt ex rel. P.M.S. v. Coons, at footnote 6, identifies the statutory channel — any reputable person, including the local welfare agency, may petition the juvenile court under Minn. Stat. §§ 260C.141 and 260C.148 — and that statutory text, not case law, is the operative authority.

Recodification warning extended to the additions. Radke, Valtakis and Grover all construe the former Minn. Stat. § 626.556, recodified in 2020 as Minn. Stat. ch. 260E; Radke's negligence holding turns on the duties that section imposed on counties, so counsel relying on it must map those duties onto the current ch. 260E provisions. M.D.O. construes the former Minn. Stat. § 260.221, and W.L.P. (2004) construes the successor provision, Minn. Stat. § 260C.301, for the same statutory grounds. G.L.H. construes the former Minn. Stat. § 260.155, subd. 2 and subd. 8(b); the opinion itself records that subd. 8(b) was recodified at § 260B.163, subd. 10(b). In re Welfare of D.L. construes the former Minn. Stat. § 259.28, subd. 2, superseded by 1992 Minn. Laws ch. 557.

Missing (for a later pass): DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services, 489 U.S. 189 (1989) — the controlling Supreme Court holding that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative duty on a state to protect a child from private violence absent a custodial relationship. Its absence is the most conspicuous gap in the brief: it is the necessary frame for FAIL-04, OUT-06 and DEC-01, it explains precisely why Burton v. Richmond turns on state-created custody, and it explains why Radke had to be pleaded as a state common-law negligence claim rather than under s 1983. A family told by this brief that Radke gives them a remedy needs to be told in the same breath that DeShaney forecloses the federal constitutional version of that claim.

Missing (for a later pass): Suter v. Artist M., 503 U.S. 347 (1992) — holds that the Title IV-E 'reasonable efforts' requirement is not privately enforceable under s 1983 or through an implied right of action. This is dispositive at FAIL-03, which the brief maps to state reasonable-efforts cases while identifying 42 U.S.C. ss 670-679c as the operative authority without disclosing that private enforcement of that authority is barred.

Missing (for a later pass): Lassiter v. Department of Social Services, 452 U.S. 18 (1981) — the Supreme Court's due-process framework for appointed counsel in termination proceedings (no categorical right; case-by-case under Mathews). It is the necessary federal counterweight to In re Welfare of G.L.H., which holds the Minnesota right is statutory only; citing G.L.H. without Lassiter leaves a practitioner unable to assess the constitutional argument at all.

Missing (for a later pass): Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023) — the Supreme Court's rejection of Commerce Clause, anticommandeering and (on standing grounds) equal-protection challenges to ICWA. Given that the brief's only Indian-preference equal-protection authority (In re Welfare of the Children of L.K. and A.S.) has been vacated by the Minnesota Supreme Court, Brackeen is now the controlling authority at INP-11 and FAIL-05 and the brief has no substitute for it.

Missing (for a later pass): Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989) — the Supreme Court's foundational ICWA decision on domicile and exclusive tribal jurisdiction. INP-11 carries six Minnesota cases and no federal anchor at all; Holyfield is the threshold-jurisdiction authority that In re Welfare of R.S. and In re Welfare of S.N.R. are applications of.

Missing (for a later pass): Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) — the Supreme Court's holding that a parent is entitled to a hearing on fitness before the state may take custody of his children. It is the constitutional origin of the process-before-deprivation rule that DEC-04, DEC-05 and INP-12 depend on, and the brief reaches those nodes entirely through Eighth Circuit cases that themselves rest on it.

Missing (for a later pass): Cracraft v. City of St. Louis Park, 279 N.W.2d 801 (Minn. 1979) — the Minnesota Supreme Court's special-duty framework for municipal tort liability. Radke is decided by applying Cracraft (and overruling Hoppe as irreconcilable with it), so a practitioner pleading a negligent-investigation claim under Radke cannot frame the duty element without it. Belongs at DEC-01, DEC-02 and INP-10.

Missing (for a later pass): Andrade v. Ellefson, 391 N.W.2d 836 (Minn. 1986) — the Minnesota Supreme Court's decision allowing a negligence action against a county for its conduct in licensing and supervising day care where children were abused. It is the direct precursor Radke relies on, and it is the case that establishes county exposure independent of the reporting statute. Belongs at DEC-02, INP-10, FAIL-04 and PMC-02, which currently has no on-point authority at all.

Missing (for a later pass): In re Welfare of H.G.B., 306 N.W.2d 821 (Minn. 1981) — the Minnesota Supreme Court's foundational statement that termination requires grave and weighty reasons, that statutory grounds are construed strictly, and that the evidence must address conditions existing at the time of the hearing. It is the ancestor of R.W., S.E.P. and T.R., and OUT-02 currently runs no further back than Santosky (1982) on the federal side and R.W. (2004) on the state side.
